power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Introduction: Accurate identification of developmental language disorder (DLD) requires assessment measures validated for their intended populations.

This study examined the psychometric properties and diagnostic accuracy of preliminary Spanish grammatical measures from the Bilingual English-Spanish Assessment (BESA) in monolingual Mexican children.
Method: Participants included 395 monolingual Spanish-speaking children aged 3;0-5;5 years (295 typically developing, 100 with DLD).

Twenty-two grammatical cloze items and 53 sentence repetition targets were examined using regression, classical item analyses, item response theory, receiver operating characteristic analyses, and repeated cross-validation.
Results: Children with DLD performed significantly below typically developing children on both tasks, while scores increased with age.
Clitic pronouns and subjunctive constructions demonstrated strong item-level discrimination, and two-parameter item response models fit better than one-parameter models.
The 21-item Morphosyntax score yielded an area under the curve of .872, compared with .847 for the 29-target Sentence Repetition score.
Combining both tasks yielded .885, although the improvement in discrimination was not statistically significant.

Discussion: Findings provide promising evidence of the diagnostic utility of preliminary BESA Spanish grammatical measures in monolingual Mexican children and highlight the importance of item-level evaluation and population-specific validity evidence.
Further research is needed to evaluate the complete published assessment, establish clinical cutoffs, and compare item performance across monolingual and bilingual populations.

Accurate language assessment depends on instruments that are linguistically appropriate, psychometrically sound, and capable of distinguishing typical variation in language development from clinically significant difficulties.
Although standardized assessments provide systematic approaches to evaluating children's linguistic abilities, their utility depends on the populations for which they were developed and validated.
Instruments developed within one linguistic context may not demonstrate comparable performance when administered to children with different language experiences or sociocultural backgrounds.

Research examining the application of monolingual assessment instruments to bilingual populations has demonstrated that using population-inappropriate reference standards can compromise diagnostic accuracy (Altman et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Research examining the application of monolingual assessment instruments to bilingual populations has demonstrated that using population-inappropriate reference standards can compromise diagnostic accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Altman et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, evaluating assessment instruments across linguistic populations is important for establishing the validity of their intended interpretations and expanding access to appropriate assessment practices.
These considerations are relevant to Spanish language assessment.
Although Spanish is spoken across diverse linguistic communities, assessment instruments with population-specific validity evidence remain unevenly available.

Instruments developed for Spanish-English bilingual children in the United States may target grammatical structures relevant to Spanish more broadly, but shared linguistic content does not necessarily imply equivalent item functioning or diagnostic performance across bilingual and monolingual populations.

Differences in language experience and developmental patterns may influence performance on particular structures, requiring empirical investigation of their psychometric properties in other populations.
Such investigations can also clarify which linguistic structures maintain diagnostic relevance across contexts and which require population-specific consideration.
In Mexico, the availability of language assessment instruments developed or validated specifically for monolingual Spanish-speaking children remains limited (Auza et al., 2024).

text.text: This creates an opportunity to investigate whether existing instruments developed for other Spanish-speaking populations can contribute to assessment practices in Mexico, provided that their diagnostic performance is established locally.

One such instrument is the Bilingual English-Spanish Assessment (BESA; Peña et al., 2018), developed to support the identification of developmental language disorder (DLD) in Spanish-English bilingual children.

text.text: Its Spanish Morphosyntax subtest incorporates grammatical cloze and sentence repetition tasks that assess grammatical abilities relevant to Spanish language development, making these components candidates for evaluation in monolingual populations rather than measures whose validity can be assumed to transfer directly.

Examining the item-level psychometric properties and diagnostic accuracy of these Spanish grammatical measures in monolingual Mexican children can provide evidence regarding their potential clinical utility while contributing to broader discussions of assessment across monolingual and multilingual contexts.

The present study examined the psychometric properties and diagnostic accuracy of the Spanish BESA Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition tasks in 395 monolingual Spanish-speaking Mexican.

Specifically, the study investigated (a) diagnostic-group and age-related differences in performance, (b) item difficulty and discrimination using classical item analyses and one-and two-parameter item response theory models, and (c) diagnostic classification accuracy of both tasks independently and in combination.
Receiver operating characteristic analyses and repeated stratified cross-validation were used to evaluate the stability and accuracy of diagnostic classification.

Through this investigation, the study seeks to extend the psychometric evidence for the Spanish BESA beyond its original bilingual population and evaluate its potential utility for identifying DLD in monolingual Mexican children who live in a different linguistic context.

The findings may also inform the selection of diagnostically informative grammatical structures and contribute to establishing an empirical foundation for using existing bilingual assessment instruments in monolingual Spanish-speaking contexts.
To address these objectives, the following research questions guided the study: RQ1.
How do monolingual Mexican children with and without DLD differ in Spanish BESA morphosyntax and sentence repetition performance, and how does performance vary by age?
RQ2.

Which items and morphosyntactic structures within the Spanish BESA Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition tasks demonstrate the strongest psychometric properties and discrimination between children with and without DLD?
RQ3.
How accurately do the Spanish BESA Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition tasks differentiate children with and without DLD?

text.text: The instrument includes measures of phonology, morphosyntax, and semantics in Spanish and English.
The present study focused exclusively on the Spanish Morphosyntax subtest, which comprises two components: Grammatical Cloze and Sentence Repetition.
These components assess grammatical production and sentence-level language abilities and are combined to derive the overall Morphosyntax score in the published assessment.
Data were collected using preliminary versions of the Spanish BESA Morphosyntax protocol administered before the instrument's final publication.
The available item pool included 22 Grammatical Cloze items and 53 scored targets distributed across eight Sentence Repetition sentences.
Consequently, the dataset permits examination of a broader set of preliminary items than those identified as retained in the published version.
The Grammatical Cloze task required children to complete elicited sentences using targeted grammatical forms.
The preliminary pool included seven article items, two preterite items, eight clitic-pronoun items, and five subjunctive items.
Sentence Repetition required children to reproduce orally presented sentences, with accuracy evaluated for specified words and phrases rather than every word in each sentence.
Across the eight sentences represented in the dataset, 53 targets were available for analysis.
Responses were scored dichotomously as correct (1) or incorrect (0).
The published Spanish Morphosyntax subtest retains the Grammatical Cloze and Sentence Repetition format but differs from the preliminary materials in item composition.
Using the item correspondence records available for the present study, we identified preliminary targets marked as retained in the final instrument (see Table 2).

Analyses were conducted at the task, item, and diagnostic-classification levels to examine group and age differences, item-level psychometric properties, and diagnostic accuracy.

text.text: Statistical significance was evaluated at α = .05, and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported where applicable.
Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition scores were calculated as the proportion of correct responses across available items and expressed as percentages.
Separate ordinary least-squares multiple linear regression models examined diagnostic-group differences in each task, adjusting for age in years and sex.
Age was mean-centered before analysis.
To examine whether age-related associations differed between diagnostic groups, Diagnosis × Age interaction terms were added to the models.
Models with and without the interaction were compared using nested-model F tests.
Regression coefficients were interpreted as percentage-point differences in task performance, and unadjusted standardized group differences were quantified using Cohen's d.
Item-level analyses examined accuracy, discrimination, and model fit across the 22 Morphosyntax and 53 Sentence Repetition preliminary items or scored targets.
Accuracy was calculated overall and by diagnostic group, with diagnostic separation expressed as the percentage-point difference between TD and DLD accuracy.
Corrected item-total correlations assessed each item's association with overall task performance, excluding the target item from the total score.
Separate Rasch models were fitted to each task to estimate item difficulty in logits and evaluate infit and outfit statistics.
Items were flagged for review when infit or outfit values fell outside 0.50-1.50, corrected item-total correlations were below .30, or TD-DLD accuracy differences were below 10 percentage points.
Items meeting none of these exploratory criteria were classified as performing well, items meeting one criterion as monitor, and items meeting two or more criteria as review.
These categories were used for descriptive screening rather than as validated clinical item-selection criteria.
Classifications were compared with the items retained in the published BESA, with published-item status determined independently of the empirical screening results.
This comparison was limited to preliminary items that could be matched to the published version and did not constitute an evaluation of every item in the finalized instrument.
To further evaluate item discrimination, one-parameter logistic (1PL; Rasch) and two-parameter logistic (2PL) models were estimated using the complete preliminary item pools.
The 1PL model constrained item discrimination to a common value, whereas the 2PL model estimated item-specific discrimination and difficulty parameters.
Model fit was compared using log-likelihoods, Akaike information criterion (AIC), Bayesian information criterion (BIC), and likelihood-ratio tests.
Expected a posteriori reliability estimates were also summarized for each model.
Item difficulty estimates and item characteristic curves were examined to compare model predictions across latent ability levels.

In the 2PL model, discrimination reflected how sharply an item differentiated individuals by latent ability, whereas difficulty represented the ability level associated with a 50% probability of a correct response.
For Sentence Repetition, item-level analyses used available responses for each target.
Because participants received different preliminary test versions, some targets were not administered to all children; these were treated as structurally missing rather than incorrect responses.

Repetition using all 22 and 53 preliminary items, respectively, regardless of their inclusion in the published BESA.
Pearson correlations between task accuracy scores were calculated for the full sample and separately by diagnostic group.
A partial correlation controlling for diagnostic group, age, and sex assessed the association between tasks beyond these participant characteristics.
Internal consistency was estimated for the Morphosyntax, Sentence Repetition, and combined 75-item pools using coefficient alpha, which is equivalent to KR-20 for dichotomously scored items.
An equal-weight global language composite was calculated by averaging participant-level accuracy scores across the two tasks.
Its ability to distinguish diagnostic groups was evaluated using Cohen's d and ROC analysis, with AUC confidence intervals estimated through 5,000 bootstrap resamples stratified by diagnostic group.
The Youden-selected threshold and associated classification metrics were also reported.
These analyses provided supplementary validity evidence within the current sample but were not intended to establish a unidimensional clinical construct.

To identify the grammatical items and structures most informative for distinguishing children with and without DLD, the second research question examined item accuracy, corrected item-total correlations, diagnostic-group differences, and item response theory parameters across the preliminary Spanish BESA Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition subtests.
The analyses also examined how psychometric performance corresponded to items retained in the published BESA.
Of the 22 preliminary Morphosyntax items, 19 met all three exploratory performance criteria, whereas two were classified as monitor and one as review.
Among the 19 items meeting all criteria, eight corresponded to items retained in the published BESA and 11 were not.
Similarly, 42 of the 53 preliminary Sentence Repetition components met all three criteria, whereas six were classified as monitor and five as review.
Of the 42 components meeting all criteria, 24 corresponded to targets retained in the published BESA, whereas 18 did not.
These categories were used to summarize patterns across the psychometric indicators rather than establish validated clinical item-selection thresholds.

text.text: Across classical item analyses and Rasch/1PL and 2PL models, most items demonstrated favorable psychometric properties, although their discriminative strength varied.
Within Morphosyntax, several clitic and subjunctive items consistently showed strong diagnostic-group separation and 2PL discrimination.
Sentence Repetition targets likewise differed in their psychometric properties, with some demonstrating substantially stronger discrimination than others.
Correspondence between item performance and retention in the published BESA was incomplete.

Several preliminary items not retained in the published measure demonstrated favorable properties, whereas article_3, an item retained in the published BESA, exhibited weak item-total association, negligible TD-DLD separation, elevated Rasch outfit, and low 2PL discrimination.

These findings identify population-and sample-specific variation in item performance and support further investigation of which grammatical targets are most informative for assessing monolingual Mexican children.
They do not establish that the preliminary items would necessarily perform better in other samples or linguistic contexts.

The third research question examined how accurately the Spanish BESA Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition tasks differentiated monolingual Mexican children with and without DLD, both independently and in combination.
Diagnostic accuracy was evaluated using full-sample receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses and repeated stratified cross-validation.
Full-sample ROC analyses indicated good diagnostic discrimination for both tasks.
The reduced 21-item Morphosyntax score excluding article_3 yielded an AUC of .872, 95% CI [.833, .912].

The 29-target Sentence Repetition score corresponding to items retained in the published BESA yielded an AUC of .847, 95% CI [.805, .888], whereas the complete 53-target preliminary Sentence Repetition score yielded an AUC of .852, 95% CI [.812, .892].

The difference between the 29-and 53-target Sentence Repetition scores was not statistically significant (p = .193), suggesting that the additional preliminary targets did not produce a detectable improvement in overall diagnostic discrimination in this sample.
Combining Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition yielded the highest full-sample discrimination.
The model combining the 21-item Morphosyntax score with the 29-target Sentence Repetition score yielded an AUC of .885, 95% CI [.848, .921].
Adding Sentence
Repetition significantly improved model fit relative to Morphosyntax alone, Δχ²(1) = 6.30, p = .012; however, the corresponding increase in AUC did not reach statistical significance (p = .059).
Thus, although Sentence Repetition contributed additional information to model fit, the improvement in overall diagnostic discrimination was modest.
Given the weak item-level psychometric properties observed for article_3 in RQ2, additional ROC analyses examined whether excluding this item improved diagnostic discrimination.
The complete 22-item preliminary Morphosyntax score yielded an AUC of .870, whereas the 21-item score excluding article_3 yielded an AUC of .872.
This difference was not statistically significant (p = .230).

Similarly, the 10 Morphosyntax items corresponding to the published BESA yielded an AUC of .848, whereas the nine-item subset excluding article_3 yielded an AUC of .856; this difference was also not statistically significant (p = .105).
Thus, although article_3 demonstrated weak item-level psychometric properties, its removal resulted in only modest changes in overall diagnostic discrimination.
These findings suggest that weak performance by an individual item does not necessarily translate into a substantial reduction in task-level diagnostic accuracy.

text.text: The present study examined the psychometric properties and diagnostic accuracy of the Spanish BESA Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition tasks in monolingual Spanish-speaking Mexican children.

The findings extend the evidence for these tasks to children assessed in Mexico and provide population-specific information about the performance of preliminary grammatical items originally developed within the BESA framework.
Three principal findings emerged.
First, children with DLD demonstrated substantially lower performance on both tasks, even after accounting for age and sex.
Second, individual grammatical structures differed in their psychometric properties, with clitic pronouns and subjunctive constructions demonstrating strong discrimination.
Third, both tasks showed good diagnostic accuracy, although combining them produced only modest improvements in overall discrimination.

Together, these results show the potential value of Spanish grammatical measures for identifying language difficulties while underscoring the importance of evaluating assessment performance within the population of intended use.
Regarding RQ1, children with DLD obtained significantly lower Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition scores than their TD peers, with large group differences observed across both tasks.
Age was positively associated with performance, consistent with previous research documenting age-related variation in Spanish morphosyntactic development (Castilla-Earls et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Age was positively associated with performance, consistent with previous research documenting age-related variation in Spanish morphosyntactic development <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Castilla-Earls et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, the absence of significant Diagnosis × Age interactions provided no evidence that these cross-sectional age associations differed between diagnostic groups.

Morphosyntax accuracy also contributed substantially to diagnostic classification, whereas age alone showed limited discrimination and did not significantly improve classification beyond grammatical performance.
These findings underscore the value of directly assessing grammatical abilities when identifying children with DLD.

Importantly, age-related differences in performance should not be interpreted as longitudinal developmental change, and the lack of significant interactions does not establish equivalent developmental trajectories.

These findings suggest that chronological age and grammatical performance provide distinct information, with direct measures of grammatical ability contributing more strongly to diagnostic differentiation in the present sample.
Regarding RQ2, the item-level analyses revealed variation in the psychometric properties of individual grammatical items.

Within Morphosyntax, clitic and subjunctive items showed particularly strong differentiation between children with and without DLD, together with high discrimination in the two-parameter logistic model.

These findings are consistent with earlier studies documenting difficulties with direct object clitics and other grammatical morphemes in Spanish-speaking children with language impairment (Bedore & Leonard, 2001 , 2005; Jacobson & Schwartz, 2002).

The present findings extend this literature by demonstrating converging evidence from diagnostic-group accuracy differences, corrected item-total correlations, and item response theory discrimination parameters in a relatively large sample of monolingual Mexican children.
The superior fit of the two-parameter models further indicated that grammatical items varied in their capacity to differentiate children along the underlying ability continuum.
This variability suggests that items targeting the same broad grammatical domain may differ substantially in the information they contribute to overall assessment performance.

In Sentence Repetition, individual linguistic targets also differed in their psychometric characteristics, reinforcing the importance of examining the grammatical components of repetition tasks rather than relying exclusively on overall scores.

Notably, strong discrimination on one indicator did not always correspond to favorable performance across all indices, illustrating the value of considering multiple psychometric criteria when evaluating individual items.

At the same time, several preliminary items not retained in the published BESA showed favorable properties, whereas article_3, an item retained in the published measure, showed weak item-total association, little diagnostic-group separation, elevated Rasch outfit, and low discrimination in the two-parameter model.

Both diagnostic groups demonstrated approximately 22% accuracy on this item, suggesting that it was difficult for children regardless of diagnostic status and contributed little to distinguishing the groups in this sample.

Its performance may reflect characteristics of the targeted structure, task demands, or the ages and linguistic experiences of the children assessed; the present analyses cannot distinguish among these explanations.
Importantly, the performance of article_3 illustrates that item difficulty and diagnostic informativeness are not interchangeable.
An item may be challenging for both groups without meaningfully distinguishing children with and without DLD.

However, favorable performance among preliminary items does not establish that they would improve the published instrument, nor does the weak performance of article_3 establish that it should be removed universally.
Rather, these findings identify candidate items for further investigation and support an empirical approach to item selection across assessment populations.
Regarding RQ3, both Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition showed good diagnostic discrimination in the present sample.

Morphosyntax yielded an area under the curve of .872, whereas Sentence Repetition yielded an area under the curve of .847, indicating that both tasks differentiated children with and without DLD, with numerically higher discrimination for Morphosyntax.

The absence of a significant improvement when additional preliminary Sentence Repetition targets were included suggests that the larger item pool did not provide a detectable advantage in diagnostic discrimination.
However, this finding does not establish equivalence between the shorter and longer item sets.
Morphosyntax performance contributed meaningfully to diagnostic classification, whereas age alone showed limited discrimination and did not significantly improve the model.
The cross-validation findings further support this interpretation.
Across the evaluated models, mean areas under the curve ranged from .846 to .875, with considerable overlap in their distributions.
Although the combined model incorporating nine Morphosyntax items and 29
Sentence Repetition targets demonstrated the highest mean area under the curve, its advantage over the other models was small.
Similarly, removing article_3 resulted in only modest improvements in overall discrimination, despite its weak item-level performance.
These findings illustrate that individual-item discrimination and overall diagnostic classification provide related but distinct forms of evidence.
An item may demonstrate limited diagnostic value without substantially reducing the accuracy of a composite score, particularly when other items capture overlapping linguistic information.
Consequently, additional studies are needed to determine whether particular item combinations consistently improve diagnostic performance in independent samples.
The high internal consistency of both preliminary item pools provides additional evidence that the items functioned coherently within this sample.
Nevertheless, internal consistency should not be equated with diagnostic validity or taken as evidence that all items measure a single underlying ability.

The strong association between Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition, including after accounting for diagnosis, age, and sex, suggests that the tasks capture related dimensions of language performance without establishing that they are psychometrically interchangeable.

Sentence repetition involves the interaction of grammatical knowledge with lexical and phonological representations and the ability to recall and reproduce linguistic structures (Komeili & Marshall, 2013; Ward et al., 2024).

More broadly, these findings contribute to understanding how grammatical measures perform across populations and assessment contexts.

Although the BESA was developed primarily within a Spanish-English bilingual assessment framework, its manual also describes use with Spanish-speaking monolingual and bilingual children and reports diagnostic classification evidence that includes functionally Spanish-monolingual children in the United
States (Peña et al., 2018).

text.text: The contribution of the present study therefore lies in providing population-specific evidence from children recruited and assessed in Mexico, rather than establishing the first application of BESA materials to monolingual children.

Previous research has emphasized that applying assessment instruments across linguistic populations without appropriate validity evidence can compromise diagnostic interpretation (Altman et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Previous research has emphasized that applying assessment instruments across linguistic populations without appropriate validity evidence can compromise diagnostic interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Altman et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: By examining both item-level properties and overall classification, the present study demonstrates an approach for evaluating the performance of grammatical measures in populations beyond those represented in their original development and standardization.

However, direct comparisons between monolingual and bilingual children would be required to establish whether the same grammatical items demonstrate comparable measurement properties across these groups.
The present findings have implications for assessing Spanish-speaking children with suspected DLD, particularly in settings where locally validated instruments remain limited.
The diagnostic performance of Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition suggests that both tasks may provide useful information about grammatical abilities in monolingual Mexican children.

However, these measures should be considered within a comprehensive assessment that incorporates language samples, caregiver reports, developmental history, and other relevant clinical information, rather than as stand-alone diagnostic tools (Peña et al., 2018).
text.formatted: However, these measures should be considered within a comprehensive assessment that incorporates language samples, caregiver reports, developmental history, and other relevant clinical information, rather than as stand-alone diagnostic tools <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Peña et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The item-level findings also highlight the importance of examining specific grammatical structures alongside overall assessment scores.

Clitic pronouns and subjunctive constructions demonstrated particularly strong diagnostic differentiation, suggesting that these structures may be informative when evaluating Spanish grammatical abilities.
Nevertheless, individual items should not be used independently to identify DLD.
Instead, patterns of grammatical performance may guide further assessment and help clinicians identify areas requiring closer examination (Peña et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Instead, patterns of grammatical performance may guide further assessment and help clinicians identify areas requiring closer examination <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Peña et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The findings also have implications for assessment efficiency and the application of existing instruments across linguistic populations.

The absence of a significant difference in diagnostic accuracy between the 29-and 53-target Sentence Repetition scores suggests that additional scored targets may not necessarily improve classification.
This is relevant to efforts to develop efficient Spanish language screening procedures (Auza et al., 2018b).
text.formatted: This is relevant to efforts to develop efficient Spanish language screening procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Auza et al., 2018b)</ref>.

text.text: However, shorter item sets require independent validation, and fewer scored targets do not necessarily reduce administration time.

More broadly, the promising performance of these preliminary BESA materials underscores the importance of establishing population-specific evidence before applying assessment norms or diagnostic thresholds across linguistic contexts (Altman et al., 2022).

text.text: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, the analyses were based on preliminary BESA materials rather than the complete published instrument.

Although some items corresponded to those retained in the published version, the resulting scores were not equivalent to standardized BESA scores, and the findings cannot establish the diagnostic validity of the complete published assessment.
Additionally, the sample included children aged 3;0-5;5 years, whereas the BESA manual specifies an age range of 4;0-6;11 (Peña et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Additionally, the sample included children aged 3;0-5;5 years, whereas the BESA manual specifies an age range of 4;0-6;11 <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Peña et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Further validation is needed for children younger than four years.
Second, diagnostic classification was established using multiple clinical and linguistic indicators, some of which assessed abilities similar to those targeted by the BESA tasks.
This overlap may have contributed to the observed diagnostic accuracy.

Furthermore, differences across preliminary Sentence Repetition versions resulted in unequal item-level sample sizes, and scoring multiple linguistic targets within individual sentences may have introduced dependencies among responses, potentially affecting item-level psychometric estimates.
Finally, the item subsets and classification thresholds were evaluated within the same sample.
Although repeated cross-validation provided evidence of internal performance, sample-informed item selection may have produced optimistic estimates of diagnostic accuracy.
The proportion of children with DLD was also higher than expected in the general population, limiting the generalizability of predictive values.

Future research should prioritize independent validation of item subsets and diagnostic thresholds, examine performance across age groups and regional varieties of Spanish, and directly compare identical grammatical targets in monolingual and bilingual children.
Such investigations would help establish which grammatical structures provide consistent diagnostic information across linguistic populations and which require population-specific interpretation.
The present study provides population-specific psychometric and diagnostic evidence for preliminary Spanish grammatical measures developed within the BESA assessment framework.

Across the three research questions, children with DLD demonstrated lower Morphosyntax and Sentence Repetition performance, clitic and subjunctive items emerged as particularly informative grammatical targets, and both tasks showed good diagnostic discrimination.
These findings demonstrate the importance of examining both individual-item properties and overall diagnostic performance when evaluating existing language assessment measures in new populations.
Although combining the tasks offered modest additional information, the broader contribution lies in identifying promising grammatical measures for further validation in monolingual Mexican children.
This work provides a foundation for continued research toward more evidence-based, efficient, and culturally and linguistically responsive approaches to identifying DLD.
